chapter: Advice to youth and the art of drumming
title: Johnny Wells at the Apex; music divided into labels
summary: They discuss Johnny Wells and the Apex Theatre band with Hines, across from the Sunset, and the New Orleans feeling in Chicago.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: There was another good drummer that I liked. Of course, I just heard him on records. Johnny Wells.
Yeah, Wells. See, he worked with Jimmy Noone Yeah, Johnny Wells was --
Johnny Wells, right, right. He was a very, very good drummer. But it was a small group thing. Jimmy Noone was making all of those things, Sweet Lorraine and all of those things.
Is different from drumming on other records that were coming out then. I know Krupa has talked about Johnny Wells.
Right, right. Well, see, they had a-- when they were working at the Apex Theatre, Earl Hines, Johnny Wells, I think, and --
Bud Scott on banjo, right. Right, right, right, and see, they were playing all of the things. And they were right across the street from the Sunset.

And Calumet, right, see, and the Sunset was there across the street. Yeah. So music has been -- in Chicago -- but it was exposed more because the people -- I don't know, maybe the people that migrated here from New Orleans still had that New Orleans feeling because they love music down there, and they loved it out here, then. But since that time, I mean, people -- it's good music, but it's very -- you've got to go and find it.
Yeah, because it's more different kinds of music.
Right, right, right. And then people have started to choosing, and this is avant garde and this is swing and this is Dixieland and so it's all divided up, the whole thing is.
Yeah, and that's to be expected with human beings, but it's unfortunate as far as music is concerned because --
Oh, right, right. If we could change, right.
